stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because slow slip events release built-up strain gradually, over days or weeks and without violent shaking, many seismologists long regarded them as a kind of safety valve for faults. Geophysicist Tomasz Rydel's analysis of two decades of GPS data from a Pacific subduction zone, however, found that four of the region's six largest earthquakes struck within months of a slow slip event on a neighboring stretch of the fault. Each of those slip events appeared to have shifted strain onto the segment that later ruptured. Rydel's findings therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: slow slip events lower the likelihood of a major earthquake on a fault.
slow slip events can move strain from one section of a fault to another.
most major subduction earthquakes are triggered by earlier slow slip events.
GPS measurements can detect fault slip that produces no violent shaking.
explanation: The old view is the 'safety valve' idea: by releasing strain quietly, slow slip events make large earthquakes less likely. Rydel found that most of the biggest quakes came soon after slow slip events that loaded strain onto the segment that then ruptured. That attacks the safety-valve reasoning directly, so the doubted idea is that slow slip lowers the chance of a major earthquake.

B.why: You picked what Rydel's data support, not what they undercut. The strain shifting between segments is the new finding, on the far side of the 'however'. It is not the old view being doubted.

C.why: You made the study's claim bigger than it is. Four quakes in one subduction zone can't show that most subduction earthquakes everywhere are triggered this way, and nothing here is doubted in any case.

D.why: You latched onto a detail of the method. Rydel's study depends on GPS picking up quiet slip, so it takes that ability for granted and doesn't question it.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires inferring that strain-shifting contradicts the safety-valve concept, with plausible distractors

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Transportation agencies have long set weight limits on aging bridges on the premise that the repeated stress of heavy trucks is what chiefly wears down concrete decks. But when civil engineer Priya Nandakumar compared 212 bridges in a northern state, she found that decks carrying only light local traffic had deteriorated at nearly the same rate as decks on busy freight routes. In both groups, the damage tracked closely with the number of winters in which the deck had been treated with de-icing salt. Nandakumar's results challenge the assumption that ______
choices: de-icing salt harms concrete decks more than freezing temperatures do.
decks treated with de-icing salt tend to show greater deterioration.
heavy truck traffic is the main cause of wear on concrete decks.
bridges in northern states deteriorate faster than bridges elsewhere.
explanation: The old assumption behind weight limits is that heavy trucks are the main thing wearing decks down. If lightly used decks deteriorate about as fast as decks on freight routes, traffic load can't be the chief cause. So the challenged assumption is that heavy truck traffic is the main source of wear.

A.why: You claimed a comparison the study never made. Nandakumar linked damage to salt treatment but never measured salt against freezing temperatures on their own.

B.why: You chose the new finding instead of the old belief. The salt pattern is what Nandakumar's data support, so it can't be the assumption her results challenge.

D.why: You stretched the sample beyond where it came from. All 212 bridges were in one northern state, so the study says nothing about how they compare with bridges elsewhere.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires recognizing that correlation with salt (not traffic) contradicts the stated assumption

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In classic planetarium experiments, caged migratory songbirds hopped toward the correct seasonal direction when shown a projected night sky, and ornithologists concluded that such birds rely primarily on the stars to steer. Recently, however, a team led by Ines Varga fitted 40 wild Swainson's thrushes with miniature radio tags. The researchers found that birds flying beneath complete cloud cover held their headings just as accurately as birds flying on clear nights. The team's results cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: thrushes rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field to steer at night.
night-migrating thrushes depend chiefly on the stars to steer.
thrushes can hold a steady heading without seeing the night sky.
caged songbirds orient correctly under projected star patterns.
explanation: The old conclusion was that these birds steer mainly by the stars. Thrushes that can't see any stars under full cloud cover still navigate as accurately as on clear nights, which undercuts the claim that stars are their main guide. The doubted idea is therefore that the thrushes depend chiefly on the stars.

A.why: You added a step the study never took. It showed that stars aren't needed, but it never tested magnetism, so it can't say what the birds use instead.

C.why: You picked what the radio-tag data show rather than what they undercut. That the birds navigate without the sky is the new evidence, on the far side of the 'however'.

D.why: You restated the old experiment's result, not the conclusion drawn from it. Varga's study doesn't dispute that caged birds oriented under a projected sky. It disputes the idea that stars are their main guide.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: the evidence directly contradicts classical conclusion with minimal inferential gap

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Flood models used by regional planners typically represent a restored wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume, which is why restoration is often promoted as a dependable way to lower downstream flood peaks. Hydrologist Kofi Mensah-Boateng's stream-gauge records from the Kessler Creek basin tell a more complicated story. While restored wetlands there did reduce peak flows during isolated storms, during a run of back-to-back storms the already saturated wetlands released runoff almost as quickly as the surrounding cropland. These records call into question the assumption that ______
choices: restored wetlands fail to lower peak flows during isolated storms.
saturated wetlands release runoff more quickly than dry ones do.
restored wetlands worsen flooding compared with nearby cropland.
a restored wetland can hold the same volume of water in every storm.
explanation: The models treat a wetland as a sponge with a fixed storage volume. The gauge records show that storage shrinks once the wetland is saturated from earlier storms. What they call into question is the fixed-capacity assumption: that a wetland holds the same amount of water in every storm.

A.why: You reversed the half of the finding that held steady. The passage says the wetlands did reduce peak flows during isolated storms.

B.why: You picked what the new records suggest, not the assumption they challenge. Saturation cutting a wetland's capacity is the new finding, not the old model's premise.

C.why: You pushed 'almost as quickly as' up to 'worse than'. At their weakest, saturated wetlands roughly matched cropland. They never did worse.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires inferring the implicit assumption about reliability across conditions, not just naming the finding

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Surveys have repeatedly found that athletes who stretch before exercising report fewer injuries than those who do not, a pattern that has made the pre-workout stretch nearly universal advice. Surveys cannot show, though, whether stretching itself is responsible. When sports scientist Lena Okafor randomly assigned 1,400 recreational runners either to stretch before every run or to skip stretching for a season, injury rates in the two groups were nearly identical, although the stretchers said they felt looser on their runs. Okafor's trial therefore undermines the belief that ______
choices: stretching before a run raises a runner's risk of being injured.
runners who stretch are more cautious in their training overall.
stretching before a run lowers a runner's risk of being injured.
stretching before a run leaves runners feeling less stiff overall.
explanation: The widely held belief, built on survey data, is that stretching prevents injuries. Okafor randomly assigned runners to groups, which rules out the problem the surveys had, and found nearly identical injury rates. That undermines the belief that stretching before a run lowers injury risk.

A.why: You flipped the claim in the wrong direction. The trial found nearly identical injury rates, so stretching didn't raise the risk either.

B.why: You filled the gap with an explanation nobody tested. The passage says surveys can't prove cause, but it never says that stretchers are more cautious.

D.why: You picked a result the trial actually recorded. The stretchers did report feeling looser, so this is supported by the new evidence, not undermined.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Identical injury rates show correlation wasn't causal.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Hail reports submitted to forecasters in one High Plains region have more than tripled since 1990, and some meteorologists have interpreted this rise as a sign that hailstorms there are growing more common. Meteorologist Dana Whitcomb examined three decades of radar data, which record hail-bearing storms whether or not anyone sees them, and found no change in how often such storms occurred. The jump in reports instead tracked the region's population growth and the spread of storm-spotting apps. Whitcomb's analysis casts doubt on the interpretation that ______
choices: hail-producing storms have become more frequent in the region.
more residents and new apps have led to more hail being reported.
storm-spotting apps alone explain the increase in hail reports.
radar measures the size of hailstones better than observers do.
explanation: The interpretation under attack is that the rise in reports means hailstorms are becoming more common. Radar, which counts hail storms whether or not anyone sees them, shows no change in how often they occur. So the doubted interpretation is that hail-producing storms have become more frequent.

B.why: You picked Whitcomb's alternative explanation, not the interpretation she casts doubt on. Population growth and apps are on the new-evidence side of the passage.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. The reports tracked both population and apps, so 'alone' claims more than the passage allows, and it is Whitcomb's side in any case.

D.why: You drifted to a side issue. The passage uses radar to count how often storms occur and says nothing about measuring hailstone size.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Reports don't track actual storm frequency.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because pollen cores from a nearby lake show a sharp drop in cereal pollen around the time the Neolithic village of Tell Varosh was deserted, archaeologists have long attributed its abandonment to a drought that ruined the village's harvests. Radiocarbon dating by archaeologist Samira Haddad's team, however, places that decline in cereal pollen roughly 150 years after the last households left the site. The new dates call into question the idea that ______
choices: Tell Varosh was occupied for about 150 years before it was abandoned.
farming near the site declined only after the villagers had departed.
the village was abandoned as a result of conflict with its neighbors.
failed harvests caused by drought drove the villagers from the site.
explanation: The old view rested on timing: cereal pollen fell as the village emptied, so drought-ruined harvests supposedly drove people out. Haddad's dates put the pollen decline 150 years after the village was already empty, so it can't have caused the abandonment. The doubted idea is that drought and failed harvests forced the villagers to leave.

A.why: You attached the number to the wrong thing. The 150 years is the gap between abandonment and the pollen decline, not how long the village was lived in.

B.why: You picked what the new dates suggest. A pollen drop after everyone left fits the new evidence, so it is not the idea being questioned.

C.why: You supplied a replacement cause the passage never mentions. Knocking out the drought explanation doesn't prove conflict, and nothing here is about warfare.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Studies of older adults have found that those who receive a flu shot are far less likely to die of any cause during winter than those who do not, and some officials have cited this gap as a measure of how many deaths the vaccine prevents. Epidemiologist Rafael Duarte noticed, however, that vaccinated seniors in his cohort also had markedly lower death rates in the weeks before influenza began circulating, when the vaccine could not yet have mattered. Duarte's observation casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: flu shots offer older adults no real protection against influenza.
the winter death-rate gap mainly reflects the vaccine's protection.
vaccinated seniors tend to be healthier than unvaccinated seniors.
vaccinated and unvaccinated seniors die at similar rates pre-season.
explanation: Officials treated the whole winter gap in death rates as the vaccine's doing. Duarte found the same gap before flu was even circulating, when the vaccine couldn't have been the reason. That points to some other difference between the groups, which casts doubt on the idea that the gap mainly reflects the vaccine's protection.

A.why: You fell for strength creep. Showing that the gap overstates the vaccine's benefit is not the same as showing the vaccine offers no protection at all.

C.why: You picked what Duarte's observation suggests, not the idea it casts doubt on. Better baseline health among vaccinated seniors is on the new-evidence side of the 'however'.

D.why: You reversed a stated detail. The passage says vaccinated seniors had markedly lower death rates before flu season, not similar ones.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Pre-season data reveals confounding not causation.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: The surviving manuscripts of Teodor Vasko's six string quartets are crowded with crossed-out passages, so historians have long portrayed these 1840s works as the products of halting, agonized composition. However, musicologist Ilse Brandt recently analyzed the inks on the pages. She found that nearly all the deletions were made in an ink Vasko began using only in the 1870s, when he was preparing the quartets for a revised edition. Brandt's findings therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: Vasko revised the quartets heavily while preparing them for a later edition.
Vasko stopped using his earlier ink because it faded faster than other inks.
Vasko struggled to settle on the music while first writing the quartets.
Vasko's revised edition of the quartets was more popular than the original.
explanation: The old view comes before 'However': the crossed-out passages showed that Vasko struggled while composing the quartets in the 1840s. That view depended on the deletions dating from when the quartets were written. Brandt's ink analysis dates them to the 1870s, which removes that support. So what's being doubted is the claim that Vasko struggled while first writing the quartets.

A.why: You chose what Brandt's evidence supports, not what it undercuts. The 1870s ink shows that Vasko did revise the quartets for the later edition. This choice sits on the wrong side of the 'However'.

B.why: You supplied a reason for the change of ink that the passage never gives. The text says when Vasko started using the new ink, not why, and how fast the inks fade isn't part of the argument.

D.why: You moved to how audiences received the two versions, which the passage never mentions. Brandt's evidence is about when the deletions were made, not which edition people preferred.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers who inspect alumina coatings on turbine parts routinely find networks of hairline cracks. Because the coatings are examined only after they have cooled from the furnace, the cracks have generally been attributed to the stresses of cooling. When a team led by Rafael Osei filmed coatings under a microscope throughout cooling, however, no cracks formed. The cracks emerged only after the coatings had sat in humid laboratory air for several days. The team's observations challenge the assumption that ______
choices: the cracks are produced while the coatings cool after leaving the furnace.
moisture in the surrounding air plays a role in how the cracks develop.
humidity is the sole cause of cracking in every type of ceramic coating.
the cracks form more quickly in dry air than they do in humid air.
explanation: The old view is that cooling causes the cracks. It rested on the fact that the coatings were only ever examined after cooling. Osei's team watched the whole cooling process and saw no cracks form, which attacks exactly that reasoning. So what's being doubted is that the cracks are produced during cooling.

B.why: You chose the conclusion the new observations point toward, not the assumption they challenge. The cracks appeared after days in humid air, so this choice is on the new evidence's side of the 'however'.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. The study looked at alumina coatings in one lab. It never showed that humidity is the only cause, or that the result holds for every ceramic coating.

D.why: You chose a comparison the passage never makes. Nobody tested cracking in dry air against humid air, so this claim has no connection to the old view the study undercuts.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Dunmore banned smoking in restaurants and bars in 2015. Over the next two years, emergency visits for childhood asthma in the city fell by nearly a fifth, and local officials credited the ban for the decline. Epidemiologist Nadia Ferro later compared Dunmore with four nearby cities that had passed no such law. Their childhood asthma visits had fallen by almost exactly the same amount over the same period. Ferro's comparison casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: asthma visits fell in cities where the laws on smoking stayed the same.
a single regional change in air quality caused every city's decline.
the ban cut adults' exposure to smoke more than it cut children's.
the smoking ban was the main reason that asthma visits fell in Dunmore.
explanation: Officials concluded that the ban caused the drop because the drop came after the ban. Ferro found the same drop in cities with no ban, which undercuts that reasoning: something other than the ban could explain the decline. What's being doubted is the officials' view that the ban was the main reason visits fell in Dunmore.

A.why: You chose a finding from Ferro's comparison. Visits did fall in the cities without bans, so the evidence supports this choice rather than casting doubt on it.

B.why: You went past what the study tested. Ferro showed that the decline happened without a ban. She didn't identify a cause, and she certainly didn't show that one air-quality change explains every city's decline.

C.why: You switched to how smoke exposure differed between adults and children, which the passage never measures. Ferro's comparison concerns whether the ban caused the drop in visits.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: No large earthquake has been recorded on the northern segment of the Varda fault in at least four centuries, so seismologists have often described the segment as locked. In this view, its two sides are stuck together, building up strain that a major rupture will eventually release. Recent GPS measurements by Haruto Mendel's team, however, show that the land on either side slides past at nearly the full rate of the surrounding plate motion, creeping steadily. These data cast doubt on the claim that the segment ______
choices: is moving gradually even though it has not produced a large earthquake.
has been storing strain that will later be released in a major earthquake.
cannot produce an earthquake of any magnitude at any point in the future.
moves far more slowly than the tectonic plates that surround the region.
explanation: The old view says the segment is locked and building up strain for a major rupture. If the sides are actually sliding past each other at nearly the full plate rate, the movement is being taken up as it happens, not stored. So the data cast doubt on the claim that the segment has been storing strain for a large earthquake.

A.why: You chose what the GPS data show. Steady creep with no large quakes is the new finding, so it sits on the wrong side of the 'however'.

C.why: You fell for strength creep. Creep makes it less likely that a large stored-up rupture is coming. It doesn't rule out every earthquake of any size, ever.

D.why: You reversed the measurement. The passage says the segment moves at nearly the full rate of the surrounding plate motion, not far more slowly.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Fatigue cracks began appearing in the steel girders of the Halvern River Bridge shortly after truck traffic on it doubled, so inspectors concluded that the heavier loads were to blame. However, strain sensors installed by engineer Lucia Okafor showed that the cracks were concentrated at girder joints that flex mainly as the steel expands and contracts with daily temperature swings. Passing trucks produced only slight strain at those joints. Okafor's findings challenge the view that ______
choices: daily changes in temperature cause the bridge's girder joints to flex.
trucks have no measurable effect on any part of the bridge's structure.
the increase in truck traffic was responsible for the girder cracking.
the cracks are spread evenly along the girders rather than at joints.
explanation: The inspectors blamed the extra trucks because the cracks appeared soon after traffic doubled. Okafor's sensors showed that the cracks sit at joints where trucks cause little strain and temperature swings cause most of the flexing. That attacks the inspectors' reasoning directly. What's being challenged is their view that the increase in truck traffic caused the cracking.

A.why: You chose what Okafor's sensors found. Temperature-driven flexing at the joints is the new evidence, so it's the side of the 'However' that's supported, not doubted.

B.why: You fell for strength creep. The sensors found only slight truck strain at the joints, which is not the same as no effect anywhere on the bridge.

D.why: You reversed a stated detail. The passage says the cracks are concentrated at the girder joints, not spread evenly along the girders.
